## Digital Marketing Agency in Pune: How Fast Should You Respond to a New Enquiry? Building a Lead Follow-Up Workflow So Paid Leads Do Not Go Cold

You should respond to a new enquiry as quickly as your business can do so reliably, and for most lead-generation businesses that means a first human or well-written automated reply within minutes during working hours, not the next day. The exact number matters less than having one: a stated response target, a named person responsible, an alert that actually reaches that person, and a record of what happened to each lead. If you are paying a digital marketing agency in Pune to bring enquiries from Google Ads, Meta Ads or search, a slow or inconsistent follow-up process wastes a share of that spend before any sale can happen. This guide explains how to build a simple follow-up workflow from form to first reply to booked conversation, using tools you may already have.

It is written for business owners and sales managers in services, education, healthcare, real estate, B2B and similar sectors where an enquiry usually needs a human conversation before it becomes a sale. It does not assume you have a CRM, though it explains where one helps. It is a process guide, not a promise of results: we do not quote conversion figures here, because they differ by industry and offer, and you should measure your own.

## Why Speed of Response Matters, and What the Evidence Does and Does Not Say

You will often see claims such as "responding within five minutes makes you many times more likely to convert". Be careful with these. Many of them trace back to older studies of specific sectors and markets, are quoted without their original method, and may not describe your customers. We have not been able to verify a single figure that applies to Indian small businesses generally, so we do not repeat one here. TODO: if you wish to cite a response-time benchmark in your own materials, cite the specific study, its date and its sample.

What can be said with confidence is logical rather than statistical:

- A person who fills in a form is usually comparing several providers at that moment. The business that replies first and clearly has a better chance of the next conversation.
- Intent fades. The enquiry made during a lunch break on a phone is a lower priority by the evening.
- A reply that arrives hours later gives the buyer time to call a competitor.
- Paid enquiries cost money to generate, so each one that is never contacted is a direct waste.

You can test this in your own business without relying on anyone's benchmark. Record the time of each enquiry and the time of the first contact, mark which leads became customers, and compare the quick-response group with the slow one after a few months. Even a spreadsheet will show a pattern.

## Step One: Map Where Leads Arrive

Before you design a workflow, list every channel through which a prospect can reach you. Most businesses have more than they think:

- Website contact form
- Landing page form for ads
- Meta (Facebook and Instagram) instant forms, if used
- Google Ads lead form assets, if used
- Phone calls from the website, the ad or Google Business Profile
- WhatsApp click-to-chat messages
- Direct messages on social platforms
- Email enquiries
- Walk-ins and referrals, which the workflow should also capture

For each channel, answer three questions: where does the enquiry land, who sees it first, and how quickly. Often the answer is "a shared email inbox that nobody watches closely" or "a dashboard that someone checks on Mondays". Our guide to the trade-offs between [Meta lead forms and landing pages](/blog/digital-marketing-agency-pune-meta-lead-ads-vs-landing-page-2026) explains how the choice of form affects the quality of the lead and the way it reaches you.

## Step Two: Choose a Response Target You Can Actually Meet

A target that nobody meets is worse than none, because it teaches the team to ignore targets. Set one by working back from your real capacity.

| Situation | A reasonable first-response target |
|---|---|
| Someone is at a desk during working hours | Within 15 to 30 minutes, tightening as the process matures |
| Enquiry arrives out of hours | An automatic acknowledgement immediately, then a personal reply at the start of the next working period |
| Phone call missed | A call back or WhatsApp message within the same working hour where possible |
| High-value or time-critical enquiry (for instance an urgent service) | Immediate alert to a named person, with a backup |

These figures are examples for planning, not benchmarks. Choose your own, publish them to your team, and review after a month of real data. If your team cannot respond quickly, it is better to say so honestly on the page ("we reply within one working day") and keep to it than to promise speed you cannot supply.

### Be honest in the acknowledgement

An automatic first reply should say what the person can expect: "Thank you for your enquiry. We will contact you by phone or WhatsApp within [your real target]." Do not pretend that the automatic message is from a person, and do not promise a callback time you cannot meet.

## Step Three: Make Sure the Alert Reaches a Human

The most common failure point in lead follow-up is not the reply; it is the notification. Check each of these:

1. **Where do form notifications go?** A single mailbox, a group alias, or the personal inbox of someone who left the company last year? Send a test enquiry from each form and watch where it lands.
2. **Do notifications reach spam?** Form emails that come from an unauthenticated sender can be filtered. Our guide to [email deliverability with SPF, DKIM and DMARC](/blog/web-development-company-pune-email-deliverability-spf-dkim-dmarc-2026) explains how to set this up so that notifications arrive reliably.
3. **Is there a mobile alert?** For fast response, an email that is read at a desk is rarely fast enough. Use a mobile notification, a WhatsApp message to the sales team, or a CRM app alert.
4. **Is there a backup?** If the named person is on leave or in a meeting, who gets the lead? Define a second recipient or a rota.
5. **Does anyone notice if alerts stop?** A broken form integration can fail silently for weeks. Send a test enquiry weekly or monthly and check it arrives.

## Step Four: Capture the Lead in One Place

Leads that sit in five places are followed up inconsistently. Choose a single list, even if it starts as a shared spreadsheet, and make sure every channel feeds it.

At minimum, record:

- Date and time of the enquiry
- Name and phone number (and email where given)
- Source: which channel and, where known, which campaign or ad
- What the person asked for, in their own words
- Who is responsible for the follow-up
- Date and time of first contact
- Status: new, contacted, qualified, quote sent, won, lost
- Reason lost, where known
- Next action and date

When volume grows, a CRM can take over this job, with automatic capture from forms, calls and WhatsApp, reminders, and reports. Our guide to [why CRM rollouts fail and how to avoid it](/blog/crm-software-india-rollout-adoption-failure-2026) explains how to introduce one without losing the team's trust. If you already know you want one, our [CRM and integration services](/services/ci-crm) cover setting up lead capture and follow-up reminders.

### Record the source properly

If you pay for advertising, source data is what lets you judge it. Make sure campaign information flows into the lead record, using consistent campaign naming and tracking parameters. Our guide to [UTM tracking and campaign naming](/blog/digital-marketing-agency-pune-utm-tracking-campaign-naming-2026) covers the conventions, and our article on [tracking phone leads from Google Ads in India](/blog/track-phone-leads-google-ads-india) covers calls.

## Step Five: Design the First Contact

The first contact has one purpose: to start a conversation, not to close a sale. Make it easy for the prospect to continue.

### Choose the channel the person chose

If someone sent a WhatsApp message, reply on WhatsApp. If they filled in a form with a phone number, a call is usually appropriate during working hours, perhaps preceded by a short message so that an unknown number is not ignored. If they gave only an email address, reply by email. Matching the channel makes a reply more likely.

### Write a reply that refers to their enquiry

A reply that repeats their question shows that a person has read it:

> "Hello Priya, this is Rahul from [Business]. Thanks for your enquiry about [specific service]. Could I ask one or two quick questions so we can give you the right advice? When would be a good time to talk today?"

Avoid long blocks of brochure text in the first message. Offer one next step.

### Ask a small number of qualifying questions

Qualifying questions help you decide how to prioritise and tell the prospect what you can offer. Three to five is usually enough: what they need, by when, rough budget or scale where appropriate, location, and who makes the decision. Make the questions relevant; an endless questionnaire discourages replies.

### Use WhatsApp responsibly

WhatsApp is the preferred channel for many Indian customers, but business use has rules. If you use the WhatsApp Business API, the platform expects customers to have opted in to receive messages, and business-initiated messages outside the customer-service window need approved templates. Pricing and policies change, so check Meta's current documentation. Our [WhatsApp flow services](/services/whatsapp-flow) include setting up opt-in, templates and automated acknowledgements correctly. Never add people to broadcast lists without permission.

## Step Six: Plan the Follow-Up Sequence

Most enquiries do not convert at the first contact. A planned sequence prevents leads from being forgotten, without pestering people.

A simple sequence for a service business might look like this. Adapt the timing to your sales cycle:

| Touch | Timing | Channel | Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Within your target | Call or WhatsApp | Acknowledge, ask qualifying questions |
| 2 | Same or next working day, if no answer | WhatsApp or SMS message | Short check-in with one clear question |
| 3 | Two to three days later | Call at a different time of day | Try to reach them |
| 4 | About a week later | Email or WhatsApp | Useful information: a relevant guide, a price range, an offer to book |
| 5 | Two to three weeks later | Short message | Final friendly check-in, with an easy way to say no |

After the last touch, move the lead to a "nurture" or "closed" status. Respect any request to stop contact immediately. Under India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 and telecom commercial-communication rules, you should have a lawful basis and honour opt-outs; confirm your obligations with a qualified adviser.

### Keep sequences human

Automate reminders for your team rather than fully automating conversations with a prospect. A reminder that says "Call Priya today about her enquiry" keeps the personal touch. Fully automated sequences have a place for acknowledgements and appointment reminders but tend to feel impersonal if used for the whole sale.

## Step Seven: Handle Missed Calls and After-Hours Enquiries

A missed call from an advertisement is a lead that may never call twice.

- **Missed calls:** log each missed call and return it in the same working period. A call-tracking tool can record the number and the source of each call.
- **Voicemail or WhatsApp auto-reply:** an immediate message such as "Sorry we missed your call. We will call you back by [time]. You can also message us here." gives the caller an alternative.
- **Opening hours in ads:** schedule call-focused ads and call assets to your staffed hours so you do not pay for calls nobody answers. Our guide to [Google Ads assets for lead generation](/blog/digital-marketing-agency-pune-google-ads-assets-sitelinks-callouts-lead-generation-2026) explains how.
- **Out-of-hours form submissions:** the automatic acknowledgement should state when you will reply, and the first task of the next working day should be to clear the overnight queue.

## Step Eight: Measure the Workflow, Not Just the Ads

Marketing reports usually stop at cost per lead. A follow-up workflow gives you the later numbers that matter more.

| Measure | How to calculate | What it tells you |
|---|---|---|
| Time to first contact | Time of first contact minus time of enquiry | Whether your response target is being met |
| Contact rate | Leads reached ÷ leads received | Whether alerts and numbers work |
| Qualified rate | Qualified leads ÷ leads reached | Quality of the traffic and the offer |
| Win rate | Customers won ÷ qualified leads | Quality of the sales conversation |
| Cost per customer | Ad spend ÷ customers won | The number the business actually cares about |
| Reasons lost | Count by category | What to fix in the offer, price or ads |

Compare these by channel and by campaign. A campaign with a low cost per lead may have a poor win rate; one with a higher cost per lead may bring better customers. Our guide to [sending lead quality back to your ad platforms with offline conversions](/blog/digital-marketing-agency-pune-lead-quality-offline-conversions-2026) shows how to feed outcomes back into Google and Meta so their systems optimise for customers, not just form fills.

### Review leads weekly

A 20-minute weekly review of new, stuck and lost leads reveals problems early. Look for leads with no contact attempt, leads waiting on you, and patterns in reasons lost.

## A Worked Example (Illustrative Arithmetic)

The following numbers are invented to show the method and are not from any client or study. Suppose a business receives 100 enquiries in a month from advertising that costs ₹50,000, so cost per lead is ₹500. Suppose that on checking the log you discover that 30 of those leads were never contacted because the alert went to an unmonitored mailbox. Only 70 were contacted.

If 20 of the contacted leads became customers, the cost per customer is ₹50,000 ÷ 20 = ₹2,500. If the alert had been fixed and the same share of contacted leads had bought, the 30 uncontacted leads might have produced roughly 30 × (20 ÷ 70), about 8 to 9 more customers, bringing cost per customer to roughly ₹1,750 to ₹1,800. The assumption that late-contacted leads convert at the same rate is generous, so treat the result as an upper bound. The point of the example is the method: find the leakage, estimate its cost with your own numbers, and fix the cheapest problem first.

## Common Mistakes

**Measuring leads, not outcomes.** An agency report showing a falling cost per lead is incomplete if nobody knows whether those leads became customers. Ask for the later stages.

**Sending every lead to the owner.** The owner then becomes the bottleneck. Assign leads to named people with a backup.

**Calling once.** One attempt at one time of day misses many people who were in a meeting. Plan multiple attempts across days and channels, within reason.

**Ignoring poor-quality leads.** Mark unsuitable leads clearly instead of deleting them, so the agency can adjust targeting. Our guide to [search terms and negative keywords](/blog/digital-marketing-agency-pune-search-terms-negative-keywords-2026) explains how poor leads can often be reduced at the source.

**Over-automating.** Customers can tell when they are talking to a script, and an aggressive automated sequence harms your reputation.

**Not testing the system.** Submit a test enquiry through every form each month and confirm that it reaches the right person, in the right format, with the right source.

## What to Ask a Digital Marketing Agency About Follow-Up

1. Do you track what happens to the leads after the form, or only up to the form?
2. Can you show us cost per qualified lead or cost per customer, not just cost per lead?
3. Will you help set up lead alerts, call tracking and WhatsApp acknowledgements, and is that in the quote?
4. How do we send lead outcomes back to Google and Meta?
5. Who checks that forms and tracking still work each month?
6. How do you treat leads that we mark as poor quality?

## Where to Start This Week

1. Send a test enquiry through every form and note where it lands and how long it takes you to notice.
2. Write a response target you can meet and tell your team.
3. Create one shared lead list with the columns above.
4. Name a responsible person and a backup for each channel.
5. Write a short acknowledgement message and a first-contact script.
6. Review last month's leads: how many were never contacted?
7. Book a 20-minute weekly lead review.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### How quickly should I respond to a website enquiry?

As quickly as you can do so reliably. For many businesses a reply within 15 to 30 minutes during working hours is realistic, with an automatic acknowledgement outside them. Choose a target you can meet, state it honestly to customers, and measure your real response times.

### Is it better to call or message a new lead?

Match the channel the person used. A WhatsApp message deserves a WhatsApp reply; a form with a phone number suits a call during working hours, perhaps with a short message first so the number is recognised. Offer a choice if you are unsure.

### Do I need a CRM to follow up leads?

Not at first. A shared spreadsheet with clear columns and a weekly review is enough for low volume. A CRM becomes valuable when leads arrive from several channels, several people handle them, or you want automatic reminders and reports.

### How many times should I follow up a lead?

There is no universal number. Many service businesses make three to five attempts over two to three weeks across different channels and times of day, then close the lead politely. Stop immediately if the person asks you to, and keep within consent and communication rules.

### Why are my ad leads not turning into customers?

Common causes are slow or missed follow-up, leads sent to the wrong place, an offer that attracts the wrong audience and unclear next steps. Check the follow-up log first, because it is the cheapest to fix, then review lead quality by campaign.
